title: Casual conversation
summary: The little endings that make Japanese sound natural among friends and coworkers: {っけ}, quotative and topic {って}, {なきゃ} / {なくちゃ}, {とか}, {じゃん} / {じゃない}, and the excuse-giving {もん}.

points.title: 〜っけ
points.meaning: (checking your memory) was it ~? ; did ~? ; (nostalgic) I remember ~
points.structure: Plain past / Noun + だった・だ + っけ ; polite: 〜でしたっけ / 〜ましたっけ
points.explanation:
{〜っけ} is added to a sentence when you're **trying to remember** something you once knew, or checking it with someone: 'What was it again?'

{明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]、何時[なんじ]からだっけ？} 'What time is tomorrow's meeting again?'

It can be a question to someone else or a question to yourself: {あれ、鍵[かぎ]どこに置[お]いたっけ。} 'Huh, where did I put my keys?'

It attaches to past forms or {だ}: {だっけ}, {だったっけ}, {〜たっけ}. For polite situations, {〜でしたっけ} / {〜ましたっけ} is fine with coworkers — {お名前[なまえ]、何[なん]でしたっけ？} is a gentle way to ask someone's name again.

With {なあ}, it can also be nostalgic: {よくここで遊[あそ]んだっけなあ。} 'We used to play here a lot, didn't we.'

examples.jp: 明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]、何時[なんじ]からだっけ？
examples.en: What time does tomorrow's meeting start again?

examples.jp: あれ、鍵[かぎ]どこに置[お]いたっけ。
examples.en: Hmm, where did I put my keys?

examples.jp: すみません、お名前[なまえ]は何[なん]でしたっけ。
examples.en: I'm sorry, what was your name again?

examples.jp: 子供[こども]の頃[ころ]、よくこの公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]んだっけなあ。
examples.en: I used to play in this park a lot when I was little, I remember.

quiz.q: 「田中[たなか]さんの誕生日[たんじょうび]、いつ＿＿？」「来週[らいしゅう]の金曜日[きんようび]だよ。」
あれ、今日[きょう]って何曜日[なんようび]＿＿？
quiz.en: Huh, what day of the week is it today again?

points.title: 〜って (quoting / hearsay)
points.structure: Plain form + って (= と言[い]っていた / そうだ) ; Noun + っていう + Noun (= という)
points.explanation:
In casual speech, {って} replaces the quotation particle {と} and much more.

- **Quoting:** {部長[ぶちょう]が、すぐ来[き]てくれって言[い]ってたよ。} 'The manager said to come right away.'
- **Hearsay** — at the end of a sentence, {って} alone means 'I heard / they say' (= {そうだ}): {明日[あした]は雨[あめ]だって。} 'Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.' {〜んだって} is very common: {新[あたら]しい店[みせ]ができたんだって。} 'I heard a new shop opened.'
- **Naming** — {っていう} = {という} ('called'): {「ミチ」っていうアプリ} 'an app called Michi'.

If you hear {って} at the end of a friend's sentence, they're almost always passing on something someone else said.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さん、今日[きょう]は来[こ]られないって。
examples.en: Tanaka says he can't come today.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]だって。
examples.en: Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 部長[ぶちょう]が、すぐ来[き]てくれって言[い]ってたよ。
examples.en: The manager said for you to come right away.

examples.jp: 「ミチ」っていうアプリ、知[し]ってる？
examples.en: Do you know an app called Michi?

examples.jp: 駅前[えきまえ]に新[あたら]しいラーメン屋[や]ができたんだって。
examples.en: I heard a new ramen shop opened in front of the station.

quiz.q: 天気予報[てんきよほう]によると、明日[あした]は雪[ゆき]＿＿。
quiz.en: According to the weather forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.

quiz.q: 「山田[やまだ]さん、何[なん]て言[い]ってた？」「少[すこ]し遅[おく]れる＿＿。」
quiz.en: 'What did Yamada say?' 'He says he'll be a bit late.'

points.title: 〜って (topic)
points.meaning: (casual topic marker) as for ~ ; what is ~? ; ~ is (really)…
points.structure: Noun / Plain form + って (= は / というのは)
points.explanation:
{って} can also mark the **topic** of a sentence, replacing {は} or {というのは} in casual speech.

{日本[にほん]の夏[なつ]って、本当[ほんとう]に暑[あつ]いね。} 'Japanese summers are really hot, huh.'

It's especially common when:
- **Asking what a word means:** {「ググる」って、どういう意味[いみ]？} 'What does guguru mean?'
- **Asking about a person or thing:** {田中[たなか]さんって、どんな人[ひと]？} 'What's Tanaka like?'
- **Giving an emotional comment about something:** {一人[ひとり]で海外[かいがい]に住[す]むって、大変[たいへん]だよね。} 'Living abroad alone must be tough.'

It's informal, but {〜って何[なん]ですか} is perfectly fine for asking a coworker what something means.

examples.jp: 「ググる」って、どういう意味[いみ]？
examples.en: What does 'guguru' mean?

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]の夏[なつ]って、本当[ほんとう]に暑[あつ]いね。
examples.en: Summer in Japan is really hot, isn't it?

examples.jp: 新[あたら]しく入[はい]った田中[たなか]さんって、どんな人[ひと]？
examples.en: What's the new guy, Tanaka, like?

examples.jp: 一人[ひとり]で海外[かいがい]に住[す]むって、大変[たいへん]だよね。
examples.en: Living abroad on your own must be hard, huh.

examples.jp: 「お疲[つか]れ様[さま]です」って、いつ使[つか]うんですか。
examples.en: When do you use 'otsukaresama desu'?

quiz.q: 「あの店[みせ]の『おまかせ』＿＿、何[なん]ですか。」「シェフが料理[りょうり]を選[えら]ぶコースのことですよ。」
quiz.en: 'What is "omakase" at that restaurant?' 'It's a course where the chef chooses the dishes.'

quiz.q: 東京[とうきょう]の電車[でんしゃ]＿＿、いつも時間[じかん]どおりに来[く]るね。
quiz.en: Tokyo trains always come right on time, don't they?

points.title: 〜なきゃ / 〜なくちゃ
points.structure: Verb (ない-form minus い) + きゃ / くちゃ (+ いけない / ならない)

examples.jp: もうこんな時間[じかん]！早[はや]く帰[かえ]らなきゃ。
examples.en: Is it already this late? I've gotta get home.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]までにレポートを出[だ]さなくちゃ。
examples.en: I have to hand in my report by tomorrow.

examples.jp: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]したら、区役所[くやくしょ]に届[とど]けを出[だ]さなきゃいけない。
examples.en: When you move, you have to file a notice at the ward office.

examples.jp: 薬[くすり]を飲[の]まなくちゃいけないのに、忘[わす]れちゃった。
examples.en: I was supposed to take my medicine, but I forgot.

quiz.q: 終電[しゅうでん]に乗[の]り遅[おく]れないように、もう出[で]＿＿。
quiz.en: I have to leave now so I don't miss the last train.

quiz.q: 来週[らいしゅう]は試験[しけん]だから、勉強[べんきょう]し＿＿。
quiz.en: The exam is next week, so I have to study.

points.title: 〜とか
points.meaning: things like ~ ; ~ or something ; (hearsay) I heard something like ~
points.structure: Noun / Plain form + とか (〜とか〜とか)
points.explanation:
{とか} is a casual way to give **examples**, like {や} but usable with verbs too, and with a vaguer feel.

- **Listing examples:** {映画[えいが]を見[み]るとか、本[ほん]を読[よ]むとかしています。} 'I do things like watching movies or reading.'
- **Softening a suggestion** ('… or something'): {ラーメンとか食[た]べに行[い]かない？} 'Want to go eat ramen or something?' Using {とか} makes it sound less pushy, because you're offering just one possible example.
- **Vague hearsay**: {田中[たなか]さん、来月[らいげつ]結婚[けっこん]するとか。} 'I heard something about Tanaka getting married next month.'

Young people sometimes overuse {とか} as a filler, but in normal use it's very natural.

examples.jp: 休[やす]みの日[ひ]は、映画[えいが]を見[み]るとか、本[ほん]を読[よ]むとかしています。
examples.en: On my days off I do things like watching movies and reading.

examples.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]、ラーメンとか食[た]べに行[い]かない？
examples.en: Want to go eat ramen or something this weekend?

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さん、来月[らいげつ]結婚[けっこん]するとか。
examples.en: I heard something about Tanaka getting married next month.

examples.jp: 疲[つか]れてるなら、少[すこ]し休[やす]むとかしたら？
examples.en: If you're tired, why not take a little break or something?

quiz.q: 日本[にほん]に来[き]たら、お寺[てら]＿＿、温泉[おんせん]とかに行[い]ってみたい。
quiz.en: When I come to Japan, I want to visit places like temples and hot springs.

quiz.q: 「お土産[みやげ]、何[なに]がいいかな。」「お菓子[かし]＿＿どう？」
quiz.en: 'What would make a good souvenir?' 'How about some sweets or something?'

points.title: 〜じゃない / 〜じゃん (confirming)
points.meaning: (casual) isn't it ~! ; you know ~ ; see, ~! (pointing out or seeking agreement)
points.structure: Plain form + じゃない / じゃん (Noun / な-adj: no だ)
points.explanation:
{じゃない} doesn't always mean 'is not'. Said with a **falling or exclamatory** tone after a plain form, it means 'isn't it!' / 'you know!' — pointing something out or asking the listener to agree. {じゃん} is an even more casual version.

{このケーキ、おいしいじゃん！} 'Hey, this cake is good!'
{だから言[い]ったじゃない。} 'See, I told you so!'

With a rising tone, {〜じゃない？} is a soft guess: {あれ、山田[やまだ]さんじゃない？} 'Hey, isn't that Yamada?'

How to tell it apart from a real negative: a real negative changes the word itself ({おいしくない}, {行[い]かない}), while the confirming {じゃない} is added after an unchanged plain form ({おいしいじゃない}, {言[い]ったじゃない}). With nouns both look the same ({休[やす]みじゃない}), so context and intonation tell you which it is.

examples.jp: このケーキ、おいしいじゃん！
examples.en: Hey, this cake is delicious!

examples.jp: だから傘[かさ]を持[も]っていってって言[い]ったじゃない。
examples.en: See, I told you to take an umbrella!

examples.jp: あれ、山田[やまだ]さんじゃない？久[ひさ]しぶり！
examples.en: Hey, isn't that Yamada? Long time no see!

examples.jp: 明日[あした]休[やす]みじゃん。どこか行[い]こうよ。
examples.en: Tomorrow's a day off, right? Let's go somewhere.

quiz.q: 「このシャツ、どう？」「いい＿＿！似合[にあ]ってるよ。」
quiz.en: 'How's this shirt?' 'Hey, it's nice! It suits you.'

points.title: 〜もん / 〜もの (casual reason)
points.meaning: (casual) because ~ (you see) ; it's just that ~ (often a childish or emotional excuse)
points.structure: Plain form + もん / もの (often だって〜んだもん) ; Noun / な-adj + なんだもん
points.explanation:
At the end of a casual sentence, {もん} (or {もの}) gives a **reason or excuse**, usually in a slightly sulky or self-justifying tone. It often comes after {だって} ('but…').

{「どうして食[た]べないの？」「だって、ピーマン嫌[きら]いなんだもん。」} 'Why aren't you eating?' 'But I don't like green peppers!'

It's related to {ものだから} (Unit 6), the more grown-up way to give an excuse.

{もん} sounds childish or cute, so it's used with close friends, family and children — never at work or with superiors. {もの} is a little softer and is often associated with women's speech. You'll hear both a lot in anime and dramas.

examples.jp: 「どうして食[た]べないの？」「だって、ピーマン嫌[きら]いなんだもん。」
examples.en: 'Why aren't you eating?' 'Because I don't like green peppers!'

examples.jp: 行[い]きたくない。疲[つか]れてるんだもん。
examples.en: I don't want to go. I'm tired, okay?

examples.jp: しょうがないよ。知[し]らなかったんだもん。
examples.en: It can't be helped. I didn't know!

examples.jp: 「また遅刻[ちこく]？」「だって、電車[でんしゃ]が遅[おく]れたんだもの。」
examples.en: 'Late again?' 'But the train was delayed!'

quiz.q: 「なんで宿題[しゅくだい]やってないの？」「だって、時間[じかん]がなかったんだ＿＿。」
quiz.en: 'Why haven't you done your homework?' 'Because I didn't have time!'

quiz.q: 「もう寝[ね]るの？」「うん、明日[あした]朝[あさ]早[はや]いんだ＿＿。」
quiz.en: 'Going to bed already?' 'Yeah, because I have an early morning tomorrow.'
